Cultural hitchhiking: burial rites and genomic variation in space and time Elisabetta Canteri 2025-07-04 Abstract Describing and interpreting cultural history and transmission has been a central focus of archaeology for over a century. New information coming from ancient DNA has revealed the fundamental role of demography in shaping both genomic and cultural change. Yet, the effects of demographic processes on the spatial and temporal distributions of cultural and genomic patterns are still poorly understood. Here, we examine the relations between demography and space-time patterns of genomic variation and cultural traditions, by testing whether shifts in genomic patterns correspond to spatiotemporal changes in burial rites. Our approach uses data accessed from the Big Interdisciplinary Archaeological Database (BIAD), linking mortuary information from approximately 4,200 individuals with genetic ancestry and mobility data inferred from over 1,300 human genomes, spanning vast parts of Western Eurasia over the last 10,000 years. By integrating and modeling these diverse datasets, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of how human mobility and demographic change intersect with cultural traditions, offering new insights into the dynamics behind culture history, and the extent to which genes and culture are transmitted in parallel.

that is not categorical (e.g., ancestry and mobility values), we have to use a regression model that is specific to angular data. This regression models both the mean direction and the dispersion simultaneously. The model assumes that a circular response variable \(\theta\) has a von Mises distribution with concentration parameter \(\kappa\), and mean direction (\(\mu\)) related to a vector of linear predictor variables according to the relationship: \(\mu + 2*atan(\beta*x)\), where \(\mu\) and \(\beta\) are unknown parameters, \(\beta\) being a vector of regression coefficients, and \(2*atan()\) being the link function. The von Mises distribution is a function of \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\), where \(\mu\) is the mean direction and \(\kappa\) is the concentration parameter. A value \(\kappa = 0\) corresponds to the circular uniform distribution; for \(\kappa > 0\), the density is unimodal and symmetrical about \(\mu\), and increasingly concentrated as \(\kappa\) increases. For \(\kappa \ge 2\) the density at the antipode \(\mu + \pi\) is effectively zero, and the distribution is well approximated by a normal distribution with variance \(1/\kappa\). We can start with an initial value for \(\beta\), to calculate \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\). These estimates can then be used to update the \(\beta\) value, and then to update \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\), analogously to the ML equations for an independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) von Mises sample. This cycle is repeated until convergence. If \(\beta = 0\), we have a null model where all observations cluster around a common mean direction \(\mu\). However, as the elements of \(\beta\) become infinite, the use of any monotone link function also leads to a null model with mean direction \(\mu ± \pi\). In such cases, the likelihood will have a peak in the vicinity of zero, and attain a similar magnitude as the elements of \(\beta\) tend to \(± \infty\). The optimization process is simplified if the x are centered at their means. So should we scale our ancestry values? (Whether we order the values or scale them, model results don’t seem to change) Further reads: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2532334?seq=2; http://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1988/1/012108 The circular package, has a lm.circular function that can be used for circular and linear data (c-l).
